title: Text extraction, OCR and layout analysis
summary: Three ways to turn a file into text: read the embedded text layer, run OCR on page images, or run layout analysis that also recovers reading order, headings, tables and figures.
useIf: Your files include scans, multi-column pages, tables or forms and you must decide how much parsing each document type deserves.
avoidIf: Every file is clean born-digital text: a heavy parser adds cost and a new failure surface for no gain.

explain.md: **Native extraction** reads the text layer already inside a born-digital PDF or Office file. It is fast and cheap, but it knows nothing about structure: columns can interleave and a table becomes a stream of cells. **OCR** reads pixels from scans and photos and returns text, still without structure. **Layout analysis** adds the structure: reading order, headings, tables, figures and selection marks.

Azure Document Intelligence layout v4.0 (`2024-11-30`, GA) returns Markdown when you set `outputContentFormat=markdown`, renders tables as HTML tables with merged cells and multi-row headers, shows selection marks as ☒ and ☐, flags handwriting per line in `styles` with a confidence, and describes figures with `boundingRegions`, `spans` and `elements`. For Word, Excel, PowerPoint and HTML it extracts embedded text only, not embedded images [[tr16]].

Inside Azure AI Search, the Document Layout skill wraps that model. `outputFormat` is `markdown` (default) or `text`, `markdownHeaderDepth` runs from `h1` to `h6` (default `h6`) and `outputMode` is `oneToMany`. Its `chunkingProperties` apply only to `text` output. It times out when a document needs over 5 minutes, and a billable Foundry resource is required beyond 20 documents per indexer per day [[tr17]]. Service limits per request are 500 MB and 2,000 pages on S0 [[tr34]].

Open-source parsers such as Docling (MIT-licensed code, runs locally, handles layout, reading order, tables and OCR for scans) cover the same ground when data cannot leave your network [[tr20]]. Quality varies by document type, which is why benchmarks such as OmniDocBench exist [[tr22]]. Treat the parser as a versioned dependency and test it on your own pages.

explain.title: Route each document to the cheapest parser that keeps its structure

whereToUse: Contracts, manuals and reports that mix prose, tables and figures and feed structure-aware chunking
Scanned archives where text is only available through OCR
Forms and invoices with selection marks and handwriting
Air-gapped or regulated environments that parse locally with an open-source tool
Pre-processing step before a Text Split or semantic chunking stage

use: Use native extraction for clean born-digital single-column text
Use layout analysis when tables, columns, forms or figures carry meaning
Use OCR-only output when scans are plain text and you do not need structure
Use a local parser when data residency or an air gap forbids a cloud service
avoid: Avoid layout analysis on every file by default: it costs more per page and adds time
Avoid native extraction for multi-column or table-heavy PDFs without checking reading order
Avoid unpinned parser versions: a silent upgrade changes chunk text and your retrieval metrics
flips: Pages are mostly charts and slides: consider a vision model or page-image embeddings instead of text parsing
Volume is very high and data must stay local: open-source parsing on your own compute beats a per-page service
You need page coordinates for citations: pick a parser that returns regions such as `boundingRegions`

pitfalls.symptom: Parsing code that read `:selected:` tokens suddenly finds no checked boxes
pitfalls.cause: Layout v4.0 returns ☒ and ☐ and tables as HTML, not the older tokens
pitfalls.fix: Update the parser code, keep a regression set of forms

pitfalls.symptom: Large PDFs fail or are billed without output
pitfalls.cause: The Document Layout skill times out after 5 minutes of layout work and is still charged when a Foundry resource is attached
pitfalls.fix: Split very long documents and filter by page count before the skill

pitfalls.cause: Native extraction read a two-column page across the columns
pitfalls.fix: Use layout analysis for multi-column files and spot-check reading order

pitfalls.symptom: Retrieval quality drops after a dependency bump
pitfalls.cause: The parser changed output (Docling v2.138.0 shipped 2026-10-12, Unstructured 0.27.25 on 2026-10-10) [[tr21]]
pitfalls.fix: Pin versions and run a parsing regression set before upgrading

scenarios.title: Mixed archive on a budget
scenarios.situation: A corpus of 300,000 files is mostly born-digital PDFs, with a smaller share of scans and some table-heavy reports. The budget is tight and answers must quote tables correctly.
constraints: Cost per page matters at this volume
A labelled test set of 200 pages exists
unknowns: What share of pages are scans or tables?
scenarios.question: How do you parse?

options.name: Route by type: native text for clean PDFs, layout analysis for scans and table-heavy files
options.why: You spend per-page money only where structure matters and verify on the labelled set.
options.tradeoff: You build a classifier and maintain two paths.

options.name: Layout analysis for every file
options.why: One path with consistent Markdown output and tables everywhere.
options.tradeoff: Pays for structure on files that have none.

options.name: OCR-only text for every file
options.why: It flattens tables and loses reading order, which breaks table questions.
options.tradeoff: Right for plain scanned prose with no tables.

flips.if: Most files turn out to contain tables
flips.then: Layout analysis everywhere is simpler and not much dearer.

flips.if: Budget is unlimited and uniform output is valued
flips.then: A single layout path wins on simplicity.

scenarios.takeaway: Route by document type and measure on a labelled sample.

scenarios.title: Sensitive documents that cannot leave the network
scenarios.situation: A team must index internal reports that policy says cannot be sent to external cloud services. Volume is moderate and layout quality still matters.
constraints: Engineers can run services on their own hosts
unknowns: What licences apply to the models the parser downloads?
scenarios.question: Which parser approach fits?

options.name: Local open-source parser such as Docling, pinned and regression tested
options.why: It runs locally, covers layout, tables and OCR, and the code is MIT licensed.
options.tradeoff: You own compute, upgrades and quality tuning, and model licences vary.

options.name: Native text extraction only
options.why: Local and cheap, and fine for born-digital text.
options.tradeoff: Tables and columns may be wrong, so answers about them degrade.

options.name: Cloud layout service with sample data
options.tradeoff: Right when residency and policy allow the service.

flips.if: A compliant private deployment of a managed service is approved
flips.then: The managed layout service reduces operations.

scenarios.takeaway: Residency can decide the parser before quality does.

quiz.q: After upgrading to layout v4.0 `2024-11-30` your checkbox parser returns nothing. What changed?
options: Selection marks are now Unicode ☒ and ☐ and tables are HTML
Checkboxes are returned only as images
The output switched to JSON only
quiz.explain: v4.0 renders selection marks as ☒ and ☐ instead of `:selected:` and `:unselected:` tokens, and Markdown tables become HTML tables. The others are not documented behaviour.

quiz.q: A 5,300 page document must be split to stay under the 2,000 page S0 request limit. What is the minimum number of requests?
quiz.explain: 5,300 divided by 2,000 is 2.65, so you need 3 requests. File size (500 MB) and the skill's 5 minute timeout also apply.

quiz.q: Which signals argue for layout analysis over native extraction?
quiz.explain: Columns, tables and forms depend on structure that a text layer lacks. Plain born-digital text is the case where native extraction is enough.

flashcards.front: How do you get Markdown from Document Intelligence layout?
flashcards.back: Set `outputContentFormat=markdown` (v4.0 `2024-11-30`, GA). Tables come as HTML tables and selection marks as ☒ and ☐.

flashcards.front: Document Layout skill: output formats and the timeout?
flashcards.back: `outputFormat` is `markdown` (default) or `text`. Documents needing over 5 minutes in the layout model time out.

flashcards.front: When does a local parser such as Docling beat a cloud layout service?
flashcards.back: When data cannot leave your network or volume makes per-page pricing hard. You then own compute, upgrades and tuning.
